purpose: Imatinib is used to treat certain types of cancer, most commonly a blood cancer called chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and a stomach or intestinal tumor called GIST. It can also treat some other rare cancers. It works best when the cancer has a specific genetic change that the drug can target.
how_it_works: Think of cancer cells like a car with a stuck gas pedal — they keep growing out of control. Imatinib works like a key that blocks that stuck pedal, specifically targeting an abnormal protein (called BCR-ABL or c-KIT) that tells cancer cells to keep dividing. By blocking this signal, the drug slows down or stops cancer cell growth without harming most normal cells.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, or upset stomach (taking it with food and a large glass of water helps), swelling in the face, hands, or feet, muscle cramps, tiredness, skin rash, diarrhea, and headache. Some people also notice weight gain due to fluid retention.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you have sudden weight gain, trouble breathing, or severe swelling, as these could be signs of fluid buildup around the heart or lungs. Imatinib can affect your liver, so regular blood tests are needed. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as it can increase drug levels in your body. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, since many drugs can interact with imatinib. Do not take it if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as it can harm the unborn baby.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is 400 mg taken by mouth once a day with a meal and a large glass of water. For some cancers or advanced disease, the dose may be increased to 600–800 mg per day, sometimes split into two doses. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your specific condition and how you respond to treatment.
